KEY MESSAGE 1...
Small low pressure zipping out of Ontario and into Quebec today
will drag a weakening cold front into the area today. This 
front will be dry, accompanied by little if any airmass change,
and will likely wash out across the area into tonight. Today 
will be the warm day of the week with highs ranging from the 
upper 50s across Northwest PA to the low-mid 60s across most of 
northern Ohio. Minimum RH values will likely fall into the 
30-40% range across Northwest OH this afternoon with slightly 
elevated westerly breezes...a reminder that the state of Ohio's 
open burn ban is in effect through November. Lows will largely 
dip into the 30s tonight, with highs in the mid to upper 50s on 
Wednesday. Rain ahead of the next system, discussed below, may 
begin encroaching on Northwest Ohio around sunset on Wednesday. 

KEY MESSAGE 2... 
The combination of amplifying ridging from the eastern Rockies
north towards Hudson Bay and a -NAO blocking pattern across the
northwestern Atlantic still supports a notable change to much
chillier and unsettled weather across the region for the second
half of the week, lingering into the weekend. Guidance remains
in good agreement on the big picture, as a trough begins to 
quickly dig into the eastern CONUS Wednesday and Thursday, with 
the trough evolving into a large closed low to end the week. 
Once this occurs, the trough/closed low will only slowly exit to
the east through the weekend and into early next week.

A cold front is expected to push across the area Wednesday 
night or early Thursday as a developing wave of low pressure 
tracks through the upper Ohio Valley. This low pressure is 
expected to transfer to off the Mid Atlantic coast on Thursday, 
as an inverted surface trough axis hangs back towards the Great 
Lakes through Friday beneath troughing aloft. There is still 
some disagreement regarding exactly how quickly this low
pressure develops and how far north/south it tracks...however, 
the overall amount of spread has decreased, with previous 
outlier models like the GFS (more amplified) and RRFS (farther 
south) coming into better agreement with the overall guidance 
suite. Surface high pressure is still on track to begin building
in from the west Saturday night into Sunday behind the trough, 
but will likely not move overhead until Monday of next week.

Rain chances quickly ramp up Wednesday night as the developing
wave of low pressure and a cold front move across the region. 
The placement and magnitude of rain Wednesday night will be 
contingent on exactly how quickly the low develops/deepens and 
where it tracks, and finer details are still to be worked out.
There are hints at a swath of more moderate rain playing out
just northwest of the developing low Wednesday night. Some 
guidance has more or less rain than our current forecast and 
further adjustments in either direction are possible. The low 
pressure exits east on Thursday so some breaks in the rain are 
expected, particularly farther west across the area where the 
majority of the day will be rain- free. However, the lingering 
inverted trough, initial north- northeast flow lake effect, and 
an embedded shortwave rotating through the region Thursday 
evening will keep opportunities for showers going, especially 
farther east across the area and south of the lake. There is 
high confidence in all precip falling as rain through Thursday, 
with lows Wednesday night mainly in the low- mid 40s with highs 
on Thursday in the mid-upper 40s. It will begin to turn blustery
on Thursday with wind gusts to 30 MPH possible.

Precipitation will become increasingly lake-driven as we get to
the end of the week and head into the weekend. Initial north- 
northeast flow will gradually turn northwesterly this weekend. 
Northwest OH will trend mainly or completely dry heading into 
the weekend while shower chances continue across much of the 
rest of the area. The higher terrain south-southeast of Lake 
Erie will see the most precip overall, with this type of flow 
supporting a spray of less-organized lake effect that favors 
the terrain. There's quite a signal among nearly all guidance 
for a Lake Huron connection bringing more persistent, organized,
and intense lake effect to a smaller portion of the area. This 
will likely set up west of Cleveland Thursday into Thursday 
night and then drift around across the Cleveland metro and 
surrounding areas Friday into Saturday, before slowly shifting 
east across the more traditional Northeast OH snowbelt through 
the weekend. Instability becomes deep over the lake Friday into 
Saturday as 500mb temperatures bottom out around -30C over the 
12-15C lake waters, so any organized lake effect will have 
intensity. The mid-levels begin gradually warming and drying 
later Saturday and beyond, meaning lake effect should begin 
loosing coverage and intensity through the second half of the 
weekend. That said, lingering lighter activity may take until
